nameStory: Caucasian comfrey gets its name from its native homeland in the Caucasus region between Europe and Asia. The word 'comfrey' comes from the Latin 'confervere,' meaning 'to grow together,' referring to the plant's traditional use in helping broken bones heal.
description: Caucasian comfrey is a robust perennial herb that forms spreading clumps in gardens and naturalized areas. This member of the borage family grows 1-3 feet tall with large, rough-textured leaves and drooping clusters of small tubular flowers. Originally from the Caucasus mountains, it's occasionally found as a garden escape in New England, though it's much less common than its cousin, common comfrey.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers hang in curved, one-sided clusters, typically blue to purple (sometimes pink or white), blooming from late spring through summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, lance-shaped leaves feel distinctly rough and sandpapery to the touch, with prominent veins running from base to tip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading clumps 1-3 feet tall, with multiple stems arising from a thick, fleshy root system

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Both stems and leaves are covered in stiff, bristly hairs that make the entire plant feel rough and scratchy when touched

habitat: Typically found in rich, moist soils in partial shade, often near old homesites, abandoned gardens, or along woodland edges where it has escaped cultivation. Prefers areas with consistent moisture and fertile soil, sometimes appearing along stream banks or in disturbed areas with good soil.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, forming rosettes of large, rough-textured foliage. Flower buds begin developing on upright stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with drooping clusters of blue to purple tubular flowers. Plants reach full size and are most easily identified.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may begin yellowing. Seeds develop but plants remain leafy until frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only thick root crowns that will sprout again in spring.

funFact: Caucasian comfrey's roots can penetrate up to 10 feet deep into the soil, making it nearly impossible to completely remove once established - even small root fragments left behind will regrow into new plants!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common comfrey, but Caucasian comfrey typically has blue to purple flowers while common comfrey usually has cream, pink, or pale yellow blooms. Both feel equally rough to the touch and have similar leaf shapes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'blue comfrey,' the flowers can actually be purple, pink, or even white. Like other comfreys, this plant contains compounds that can be toxic if consumed, so it's best admired rather than used medicinally despite its traditional reputation as a healing herb.
compareHints: Compared to common comfrey, Caucasian comfrey is generally smaller and more likely to have blue or purple flowers rather than cream or yellow ones. Rough comfrey is taller and more robust than both, with larger leaves and a more aggressive spreading habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common comfrey is much more robust and taller than its relatives rough comfrey and Caucasian comfrey.
Rough comfrey stands taller than common comfrey and has much more aggressive, scratchy hairs on its leaves and stems.
